title: XOR Properties and the Single-Number Family
summary: XOR's self-canceling property — a value XORed with itself vanishes — turns an entire family of "find the odd one out" problems into an O(1)-space, single-pass trick. Learn the three properties, where they generalize, and where they quietly stop applying.

slides.markdown:
XOR has one property no other bitwise operator has: **a value XORed with itself becomes zero**, and a value XORed with zero is unchanged. Combine those two facts with the fact that XOR doesn't care what order you apply it in, and you get a way to make every *paired* value in a collection cancel out, leaving only whatever didn't have a partner.

That single idea solves the entire **Single Number** family — find the one element that appears an odd number of times, or the two elements that are unique — in O(1) extra space, no hash set required. This topic is about knowing exactly when that trick applies and when it quietly doesn't.

Everything in this topic reduces to three facts about XOR:

- **a ^ a = 0** — anything XORed with itself cancels to zero. This is the self-canceling property that does all the work.
- **a ^ 0 = a** — XOR with zero is the identity operation, so a lone unpaired value passes through untouched.
- **XOR is commutative and associative** — `a ^ b ^ c` gives the same result no matter what order you XOR them in, or how you group the parentheses.

The third property is what makes the trick practical: it means you can XOR an entire array together in any order — one linear pass, no sorting, no extra structure — and every value that has a partner will find it and cancel, regardless of where in the array that partner sits.

slides.sectionTitle: Folding an array down to the survivor
slides.markdown:
Take `[4, 1, 2, 1, 2]`. XOR them left to right: `4 ^ 1 = 5`, `5 ^ 2 = 7`, `7 ^ 1 = 6`, `6 ^ 2 = 4`. The two 1s cancelled each other out somewhere in the middle, the two 2s cancelled out, and what's left is `4` — the only element without a partner — even though the pairs weren't adjacent.

The order didn't matter and the pairs didn't need to be next to each other; associativity and commutativity guarantee every matching pair finds its cancellation regardless of position. This is the entire mechanism behind Single Number I, and it runs in one pass with a single accumulator variable.

slides.subTitle: Every element appears twice except one
slides.markdown:
```python
def single_number(nums):
    result = 0
    for x in nums:
        result ^= x       # paired values cancel; the loner survives
    return result
```

O(n) time, **O(1) space** — no hash set counting occurrences. Compare that to the hash-map approach: count every value, then scan for the count of 1 — correct, but O(n) space for the counts. The XOR fold gets the same answer with a single integer accumulator, which is exactly why it's the answer interviewers are fishing for when they say "can you do this without extra space?"

slides.subTitle: Every element appears three times except one
slides.markdown:
Change "twice" to "three times" and the plain XOR fold **breaks completely** — XOR three identical copies of `x` together and you get `x` back (`x ^ x ^ x = x`, since the first two cancel), not zero, so a tripled value pollutes the result instead of vanishing.

The fix has to think per-bit instead of per-element: for each of the 32 bit positions, **sum how many numbers have a 1 there**. Any position where three copies of a tripled value contributed is a multiple of 3 by construction; only the singleton value's bits break that pattern. Taking each bit-sum modulo 3 recovers exactly the singleton's bits.

```python
def single_number_ii(nums):
    result = 0
    for bit in range(32):
        count = sum((x >> bit) & 1 for x in nums)
        if count % 3:
            result |= (1 << bit)
    return result
```

Still O(1) space, still O(n) time (32 passes over n is still O(n)), but the technique is genuinely different — per-bit counting, not a fold.

slides.subTitle: Two unique elements instead of one
slides.markdown:
Now suppose **two** elements are unique and everything else appears twice. A plain XOR fold of the whole array gives `unique1 ^ unique2` — both survivors are in there, tangled together, and you can't separate them from one combined value alone.

The trick: since `unique1 != unique2`, their XOR is nonzero, so **at least one bit differs between them**. Pick any bit where the combined XOR has a 1 — call it the distinguishing bit — and split the entire array into two groups by whether each number has that bit set or not. Every paired value has an identical twin, so both copies always land in the *same* group and cancel there. The two uniques, differing at that bit, are guaranteed to land in **different** groups. XOR-fold each group separately and you get `unique1` and `unique2` cleanly separated.

The distinguishing bit is usually taken as the lowest set bit of the combined XOR, via `combined & -combined`, which isolates it in one operation.

slides.sectionTitle: Finding a missing number via XOR
slides.markdown:
Given an array containing `n` distinct numbers from `0..n` with exactly one missing, XOR gives an O(1)-space alternative to the obvious sum formula:

```python
def missing_number(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    result = n              # start with the one "extra" expected value
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        result ^= i ^ x
    return result
```

XOR every index `0..n-1` and every value in `nums` together, plus `n` itself for the range's top end. Every value that *is* present cancels with its matching index-XOR contribution, leaving only the missing number. The sum-based formula (`n*(n+1)/2` minus the actual sum) works too and is arguably more obvious, but it can silently **overflow** on large `n` in fixed-width integer languages, where XOR never overflows because it never produces a value larger than the widest input.

Every trick on this topic depends on one assumption: **duplicates come in exact, complete pairs** (or exact triples for Single Number II). Reach for a plain XOR fold when that assumption doesn't hold and you get a confidently wrong answer with no error to warn you.

Concretely, XOR folding gives nonsense if: a value appears an **even number of times but more than twice** (say, four times) mixed with a singleton — the four copies still cancel to 0, so that part works, but if you assumed "appears twice" and someone's input actually has a value appearing four times, your mental model of what's being tested is wrong even though the arithmetic happens to still work. More dangerously: if the *count pattern itself is unknown or mixed* (some values twice, some three times, in the same array), no single fold or modulo scheme recovers a unique answer at all — you'd need the general per-bit or hash-based approach.

Always confirm the exact duplication pattern the problem guarantees before reaching for XOR; it's a precise tool for a precise shape of input, not a general "find the odd one out" hammer.

slides.subTitle: Worth recognizing, not worth using
slides.markdown:
You can swap two variables without a temporary: `a ^= b; b ^= a; b ^= a; a ^= b;` — no wait, the real sequence is `a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b;`. Trace it through and it genuinely swaps `a` and `b` using only XOR, exploiting the same self-canceling property as everything else on this topic.

Recognize it because interviewers occasionally ask "can you spot what this does," but don't reach for it in real code: it **silently corrupts data if `a` and `b` are the same variable or alias the same memory location** (`a ^= a` zeroes it out on the first line, destroying both), it has zero performance benefit on any modern compiler (which already optimizes a normal swap into a register exchange), and it is meaningfully harder to read than `a, b = b, a`. This is a curiosity for pattern recognition, not a habit worth keeping.

slides.sectionTitle: Why this shows up outside puzzles
slides.markdown:
XOR's cancel-a-pair property isn't just a coding-puzzle curiosity — **network protocols use it for cheap error detection**, and **distributed systems use it for reconciliation**. A parity bit is literally the XOR of a block's other bits; RAID 5 storage reconstructs a lost disk by XORing the surviving disks together, because XOR is its own inverse — the same operation that combined the data recovers it.

It also shows up in **streaming "find the difference" problems** at scale: given two massive logs of IDs where one is almost identical to the other except for a handful of additions, XOR-folding both streams into a running accumulator finds the differing IDs in O(1) memory, without ever holding either full log in a hash set.

The generalizable lesson isn't "memorize the Single Number variants" — it's **recognize when a problem's structure is "pairs cancel, singles survive"** and reach for XOR before a hash set. The next topic, Bit-Counting Tricks, reuses the same per-bit thinking from Single Number II — counting something per bit position rather than per element — to build a fast popcount and a one-line power-of-two check.
